titleText.es: Hasta ahora estoy contento con mi Kindle 2, pero si cortan el acceso gratuito a la Wikipedia, pienso plantarme en el césped de Jeff Bezos borracho y negándome a irme.
titleText.en: I'm happy with my Kindle 2 so far, but if they cut off the free Wikipedia browsing, I plan to show up drunk on Jeff Bezos's lawn and refuse to leave.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive closely translates the official title text. Kindle, Wikipedia, and Jeff Bezos are proper names in this metadata rather than comic-image vocabulary targets.

excludedUnits.rationale: Kindle is the proper product name of Amazon's e-reader, not a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: LOS EBOOKS SON PARA LOS IMBÉCILES.

excludedUnits.rationale: Kindle is the proper product name of Amazon's e-reader, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Qué carries a written accent because it directly asks for the device's purpose after para.

regions.labelEs: ACCESO MÓVIL A LA WEB GRATIS. AUNQUE ME PASE MESES BORRACHO Y SIN BLANCA EN UNA CIUDAD EXTRAÑA, TODAVÍA PODRÉ SEGUIR USANDO LA WIKIPEDIA Y WIKITRAVEL PARA ENTERARME DE TODO LO QUE NECESITO.

excludedUnits.rationale: Wikipedia is the proper name of the online encyclopedia, not a Spanish lexical word.
Wikitravel is the proper name of a travel-information website, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Acceso names availability, a introduces the resource, and la web fills that resource slot; móvil only describes the kind of access.
Acceso names the thing first, and móvil follows it as the neutral description.
Móvil stays singular to match acceso and has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.
Aunque presents a possible concession, me belongs to the pronominal verb, and pase is the special uncertain form rather than ordinary paso.

applications.exampleEs: ME PASE MESES BORRACHO Y SIN BLANCA
applications.explanationEn: Me and pase form pasarse for the speaker, meses supplies the duration, and borracho and sin blanca supply two coordinated conditions.
Sin and blanca form the fixed informal money expression; blanca remains feminine singular as part of the idiom.
Ciudad names the place first, and extraña follows it as the neutral description.
Extraña uses its feminine singular form to match the feminine singular noun ciudad.
Podré is poder's first-person future form: the irregular future base podr- takes the ending -é for the speaker.
Podré changes for the speaker and future time, while seguir stays in its unchanged dictionary form as the action made possible.
Seguir supplies the idea of continuing, and usando is usar's ongoing -ando form.
Para introduces the purpose, and enterarme keeps enterar in its unchanged dictionary form with me attached.
Enterar remains in its unchanged dictionary form, and me is attached directly to its end to match the speaker.

applications.exampleEs: ENTERARME DE TODO LO QUE NECESITO
applications.explanationEn: Enterarme gives the speaker's form, de introduces what is learned, and todo lo que necesito fills the information slot.
Lo and que work together to introduce an unnamed thing rather than a masculine noun.
Qué carries a written accent because it directly asks for the source of the familiar feeling after de.
Me marks the speaker as the person with the familiar feeling, suena agrees with the singular thing, and eso names that thing after the verb.
Da is dar's irregular positive command for one familiar listener.
Da is dar's positive command for one familiar listener, and me is attached at the end for the recipient.

excludedUnits.rationale: Amazon Kindle is a joined stylized brand and product name, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Rasca is the positive command form of rascar for one familiar listener.
This repeated rasca is again the positive command form for one familiar listener.
The third rasca repeats the same positive informal command form.
Autoestopista names the person first, and galáctico follows it as the neutral description.
Autoestopista has the same noun form for a man or woman; galáctico is masculine singular here and shows that this phrase is grammatically masculine.

cards.noteEn: Ebook is an English loan used in Spanish for a book read on an electronic device. The printed plural ebooks adds -s.

example.en: I read e-books on the train.

cards.answerEn: huh?; eh? (a skeptical or surprised echo)
cards.noteEn: Eh can repeat or react to what was just said. The questioning tone can show surprise, doubt, or mild skepticism rather than hesitation.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; Spanish uses the article before a general group
cards.noteEn: Spanish normally uses los before a plural group discussed as a whole, as in los programadores. English often leaves “the” out and simply says “programmers” when making the same general statement.
Para can introduce the person, animal, or thing that something is meant for. This differs from para before an action verb, where it expresses a purpose such as “in order to.”
Imbécil can describe a person as very foolish and is normally insulting. The plural imbéciles carries a written accent.

cards.answerEn: for what purpose; what for (before qué)
cards.noteEn: In para qué, para asks about the goal or use of something. Qué keeps its written accent because it is asking a question.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.answerEn: access; entry; permission to use something
cards.noteEn: Acceso can refer to physical entry or permission to use a system, account, or resource.

example.es: No tengo acceso a esa cuenta.
example.en: I do not have access to that account.

cards.questionEn: How do you connect acceso to the place, service, or resource that can be reached or used?
cards.answerEn: Use acceso followed by a, then name the place, service, or resource.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by,” and recurso means the thing available for use. Keep a after acceso: acceso a internet, acceso a la cuenta, or acceso al edificio. Al is the combined form of a + el.

example.es: Los estudiantes tienen acceso al laboratorio.
example.en: The students have access to the laboratory.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.answerEn: mobile; available through a mobile device or network
cards.noteEn: Here móvil is an adjective describing a kind of access, not the noun used in Spain for a cell phone. It has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

cards.answerEn: to; introduces the place, service, or resource being accessed
cards.noteEn: Acceso is normally followed by a before the thing that someone can reach or use: acceso a internet, acceso al edificio. A and el combine as al.

example.en: We have access to the library.

cards.noteEn: Web is an English loan commonly used as a feminine noun in Spanish, as in la web. It can refer to the World Wide Web or to a website, depending on context.

example.es: Encontré la información en la web.
example.en: I found the information on the web.

cards.noteEn: Gratis does not change for gender or number.

cards.promptEs: aunque + presente de subjuntivo para una posibilidad incierta
cards.questionEn: How do you say “even if” when the condition is possible but not being stated as a fact?
cards.answerEn: Use aunque, then put the uncertain action in its special subjunctive form.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” The subjunctive is a special verb form used when the speaker does not present the condition as an established fact. For example, ordinary llueve becomes llueva, and paso can become pase. Use an ordinary form after aunque when you mean “although” and treat the event as a fact.

example.en: Even if it rains, we will go out.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone spends a length of time in a certain state?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of pasarse, state the duration, then add the word describing the person's condition.
cards.noteEn: The plus signs mean “followed by,” período means the length of time, and estado means the condition. Pasarse uses me, te, se, nos, or os to match the person; only the verb changes for time and person. A describing adjective also matches that person when its form changes.

example.es: Ana se pasó dos días enferma.

cards.answerEn: I spend; I may spend (a length of time)
cards.noteEn: With me, pase comes from pasarse and describes spending time in a state or activity. The ordinary present form paso changes to pase after a trigger such as aunque when the situation is treated as uncertain rather than stated as fact.

example.es: Aunque me pase una semana enfermo, terminaré el trabajo.
example.en: Even if I spend a week sick, I will finish the work.

cards.questionEn: What informal Spanish expression says that someone has no money at all?
cards.answerEn: Use sin blanca to mean “without a penny” or “completely broke.”
cards.noteEn: This is a fixed colloquial expression, especially associated with Spain. A blanca was once a low-value coin, so the expression pictures someone as lacking even the smallest amount of money. Do not change blanca to match the person.

example.es: Después del viaje se quedó sin blanca.
example.en: After the trip, he was completely broke.

cards.answerEn: a penny; any money (in sin blanca)
cards.noteEn: A blanca was an old coin. In the fixed informal expression sin blanca, the word now contributes the idea of not having even the smallest amount of money.

example.en: I got home without a penny.

cards.noteEn: Podré is the future form of poder for the speaker. Poder uses the shortened future stem podr-, and the ending -é supplies both “I” and “will.”

example.en: Tomorrow I will be able to help you.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone keeps doing or continues an activity?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of seguir followed by the activity verb in its -ando or -iendo form.
cards.noteEn: Seguir changes for the person and time; the following activity form stays unchanged. For example, mover becomes moviendo and estudiar becomes estudiando.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.answerEn: to find out; to learn about something
cards.noteEn: Enterarme joins the dictionary form enterar with me. In this pronominal use, enterarse de means to become informed or find something out; it does not mean to put something inside.

example.en: I want to find out about the news.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone finds out about or learns something?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of enterarse, then de, then state the information or subject learned.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” Enterarse is used with a short person marker: me entero, te enteras, se entera, nos enteramos, os enteráis, or se enteran. Keep de before the fact, news, event, or topic, even where English simply says find out.

example.es: Nos enteramos de la noticia ayer.
example.en: We found out about the news yesterday.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; required after enterarse before the information
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses enterarse de before the fact, news, or subject learned. The de remains even when natural English uses only find out.

example.en: She found out about the change.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “what” or “the thing that” without naming a specific object?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que to refer to an idea, action, situation, or unnamed thing.
cards.noteEn: Here lo is neutral: it does not stand for a masculine noun. Que introduces the information that identifies the idea or thing. Together they work as one unit.

example.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something sounds familiar to someone?
cards.answerEn: Name the thing, use me, te, le, nos, os, or les for the person, then use the matching form of sonar.
cards.noteEn: The plus signs mean “used together,” algo stands for the familiar thing, and the slash marks a choice among the short person words. The thing controls the verb: ese nombre me suena, but esos nombres me suenan. Spanish can also put the thing after the verb.

example.en: That song sounds familiar to me.

cards.noteEn: Suena is a present form of sonar. With me, te, le, nos, os, or les, it can say that a name, idea, or thing feels familiar to someone.

example.en: That name sounds familiar to me.

cards.noteEn: Dame joins da, the positive command of dar for one familiar listener, with me for the recipient. Positive commands attach short words such as me to the end.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?

cards.noteEn: Rasca is the positive command of rascar for one familiar listener. It has the same written form as the ordinary present form used with él or ella.

cards.answerEn: The scratched device reveals a reference to The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.
cards.noteEn: Douglas Adams's science-fiction series features an electronic guide containing vast amounts of useful travel information. A wirelessly connected e-reader resembles that fictional guide, so scratching away the Kindle branding uncovers the joke's imagined true identity.
Autoestopista names a person who travels by getting free rides from passing vehicles. The same noun form can refer to a man or a woman.

example.es: El conductor recogió a una autoestopista.
example.en: The driver picked up a hitchhiker.

cards.noteEn: Galáctico describes something related to a galaxy. The feminine form is galáctica, and the plural forms are galácticos and galácticas.
